This effect was weaker when the conflict was revealed by an outside source rather than by the adviser and when participants could make their decisions privately. These results suggest that participants followed the disclosed advice largely because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: learning of the conflict from the adviser made the advice seem more credible than it would have seemed if an outside source had revealed it.
making their choices in private freed them to accept advice that they would have been reluctant to accept in front of the adviser.
the disclosures were too brief for them to understand how the adviser’s interests might affect the advice they received.
they felt pressure to help an adviser who had personally told them about a stake in their decision.
items.explanation: The effect was weaker when someone other than the adviser revealed the conflict and when participants could choose privately, so it depended on the adviser’s having personally revealed the stake and on the adviser’s seeing the choice. That points to a felt obligation to help the adviser rather than to trust in the advice, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says disclosure lowered trust in the advice, so the adviser’s own disclosure did not make the advice more credible.

B.why_wrong: The text says the effect was weaker when participants could choose in private, so privacy made them less likely, not more likely, to follow the advice.

C.why_wrong: Participants’ lower trust shows that they did grasp what the conflict meant, and nothing in the text suggests the disclosures were hard to understand.

sources.what: Sah, Loewenstein, Cain 2013 (JPSP): six experiments; disclosure decreased trust in advice but increased pressure to comply when advisees felt obliged to satisfy the adviser’s personal interests; the pressure was reduced when the disclosure came from an external source, was not common knowledge, the advisee could change their mind later, or the decision was made privately

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology, behavioral economics). Steps: (1) the two moderators show compliance tracks the adviser’s personal disclosure and the adviser’s seeing the choice; (2) with trust lowered, that leaves a felt obligation to the adviser. Kept premises: A the source condition, B the privacy condition, C participants and the disclosure.

band7.why: The two moderators must be read together (adviser’s own disclosure, adviser sees the choice) and lowered trust rules out credibility; A and B each keep one moderator and break the link, C a rival cause. Strong band 6, near band 7.

items.subtype: T1 rejects a premise: non-native animal plus early burial dates a relationship
items.passage: Ancient Egyptians are generally credited with domesticating cats, having begun breeding them approximately 4,000 years ago. Wildcats, however, are not native to the Mediterranean island of Cyprus, so feline bones excavated at early settlements there indicate that people transported the animals from the mainland. In 2004, archaeologist Jean-Denis Vigne and colleagues reported that at Shillourokambos, a Neolithic farming village on Cyprus, they had uncovered a wildcat that had been interred roughly 9,500 years ago alongside a human, accompanied by seashells, polished stones, and other offerings. Considered together, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: wildcats reached Cyprus on their own long before people did and were later tamed by the island’s first farming communities.
people had formed close ties with cats thousands of years before Egyptians are thought to have begun breeding them.
cats had already been domesticated in Egypt by about 9,500 years ago and were carried from there to Cyprus.
the people of Shillourokambos valued cats chiefly for protecting their stores of grain from mice.
items.explanation: Since cats are not native to Cyprus, people must have carried them to the island, and a wildcat buried beside a person with offerings 9,500 years ago points to a close bond. That is about 5,500 years before Egyptians are thought to have begun breeding cats, so close relationships between people and cats began much earlier, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says wildcats are not native to Cyprus and that people brought them from the mainland.

C.why_wrong: The text dates Egyptian cat breeding to about 4,000 years ago and identifies the buried cat as a wildcat, so nothing supports domestic Egyptian cats on Cyprus 9,500 years ago.

D.why_wrong: The text gives no information about grain or mice; the burial beside a person with offerings points to a close bond, not to pest control.

sources.what: Vigne et al. 2004 (Science): about 9,500 years ago a human, a cat (Felis silvestris) and offerings were buried together at Shillourokambos, Cyprus; cats were non-native and brought by people from the mainland; Egyptians generally thought first to domesticate cats about 4,000 years ago

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. Steps: (1) not native, so people transported the cats; burial beside a person with offerings shows a close bond; (2) 9,500 years ago is thousands of years before the Egyptian date, so the received start date is wrong. Key worded as close ties, not domestication (source: taming). Kept premises: A tamed cats on Cyprus, C cats carried to Cyprus, D people valued cats.

band7.why: S3 rejection of the received date by chaining non-native status, burial with offerings and the Egyptian date; A and C partly right (taming on Cyprus, cats carried to Cyprus), D a plain OUT. Strong band 6.

items.subtype: T4 X but not Y: two interference tasks dissociate two groups
items.passage: Practitioners of the mental abacus, a technique taught in parts of Asia, solve arithmetic problems by visualizing an abacus and imagining manipulating its beads. Psychologists Michael Frank and David Barner asked trained practitioners and participants without such training to calculate while simultaneously performing a second task. Repeating words from a recording made calculation nearly impossible for the untrained participants but only slightly disrupted the abacus users, whereas drumming their fingers had no effect on the untrained participants but disrupted the abacus users about as much as repeating words did. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the abacus users depend less than other people on words when calculating and may draw partly on hand movements instead.
the abacus users are disrupted less than untrained people are by any task they perform while calculating.
untrained people rely more heavily on hand movements than abacus users do when they solve arithmetic problems.
repeating words is more disruptive than drumming one’s fingers for anyone who is trying to calculate mentally.
items.explanation: Repeating words barely affected the abacus users but nearly stopped the untrained participants, so the abacus users rely much less on words. Finger drumming disrupted only the abacus users, which suggests that their calculations may involve movement, as with a real abacus. A states both points.

B.why_wrong: This holds for repeating words but not for finger drumming, which disrupted the abacus users and had no effect on the untrained participants.

C.why_wrong: Finger drumming had no effect on the untrained participants and disrupted the abacus users, the reverse of what this choice claims.

D.why_wrong: This was true only of the untrained participants; for the abacus users, finger drumming was about as disruptive as repeating words.

sources.what: Frank and Barner (JEP: General 2012) as reported by Discover: verbal interference (repeating words from a recording) made calculation almost impossible for untrained subjects but only slightly perturbed mental abacus users; finger drumming had no effect on untrained subjects but disturbed abacus users to a similar slight extent; users not calculating verbally, motor memory may be involved; checked on the Wayback Machine copy (live page unreachable)

items.notes: Area: social science (cognitive psychology). Verbal result also in the primary abstract (Frank and Barner 2012, PubMed 21767040: practiced users, not controls, relatively insensitive to verbal interference); motor result from the cited report. Steps: (1) verbal task spares abacus users, so little reliance on words; (2) motor task hurts only them, so movement may be involved. Key hedged (may) as the source is. Kept premises: B abacus users resisted the verbal task, C hand movements matter for one group, D the verbal task hurt the untrained group.

fixes: ‘had trained practitioners ... calculate’ (read first as past perfect) changed to ‘asked trained practitioners ... to calculate’
B reworded to relative disruption (‘disrupted less ... by any task’): as written it claimed absolute accuracy, which the text does not report

band7.why: Double dissociation over two groups and two tasks; B, C and D each keep one true cell and break one link (B reworded to be wrong on the stated data). Strong band 6.

items.subtype: T2 implication: scholar’s rejection of a reading practice
items.passage: Readers of the Shijing, a collection of Chinese poems more than 2,500 years old, traditionally practiced xieyin: whenever a line failed to rhyme, they altered the customary pronunciation of a word to accommodate the rhyme. In the early 1600s, scholar Chen Di rejected this practice after systematically analyzing the rhymes of the Shijing and other ancient texts, contending that pronunciation inevitably changes over time. Chen’s argument implies that the lines that seemed not to rhyme ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: were written by poets who regarded loose or approximate rhymes as acceptable in certain kinds of verse.
should be read with the altered pronunciations that earlier readers used, since those preserved the poems’ original sounds.
most likely rhymed in the speech of the poets’ own era, before the pronunciation of some words shifted.
contain errors introduced by later copyists who altered the wording of the poems over the centuries.
items.explanation: Xieyin treated a failed rhyme as something to fix by changing a word’s pronunciation case by case. Chen Di rejected that practice on the ground that pronunciation changes over time, which implies that the lines rhymed when the poems were composed and only seem not to rhyme because the words are now pronounced differently, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Chen explains the problem by changes in pronunciation over time, not by poets’ tolerance for imperfect rhymes.

B.why_wrong: Chen rejected xieyin, so his argument does not support reading the poems with the altered pronunciations it produced.

D.recipe: change moved from sound to text (MIX)
D.why_wrong: Chen’s argument concerns change in the sounds of words, not in the poems’ wording; the text says nothing about copyists.

sources.what: Chen Di (1541–1617): xieyin changed the usual reading of a character in a Shijing poem to suit the rhyme; through analysis of the rhymes of the Shijing and other ancient rhymed texts he rejected xieyin and showed Old Chinese had its own sound system, holding that characters evolve and sounds change

items.notes: Area: humanities (linguistics, literature). Chen’s view paraphrased without quotation marks. Steps: (1) xieyin treats nonrhymes as fixable case by case; (2) if sounds change over time, the nonrhymes come from later pronunciation, so the lines once rhymed. Kept premises: A the poets, B the original sounds, D change over time.

band7.why: T2 implication of Chen’s argument (sounds change, so the lines once rhymed); A rival explanation, B practice endorsed, D change moved to the text. Short passage (76 words) and one main step: band 6 at best.

items.subtype: T1 controlled comparison: equal results across match ratios
items.passage: Charities frequently announce that a major donor will match contributions, on the assumption that people give more readily when each dollar they donate generates additional money for the cause. In a field experiment, economists Dean Karlan and John List mailed fundraising letters to more than 50,000 previous donors to a nonprofit organization. Some letters mentioned no match, whereas others offered to match each dollar contributed with one, two, or three additional dollars. Letters offering a match generated more revenue per letter than letters offering none, but the $2 and $3 matches generated no more than the $1 match did, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: a $1 match is the most effective offer a charity can make, because larger matches discourage donors who would have given without any match.
donors responded to the presence of a match much more than to how much it would add to each of their gifts.
the larger matches failed to raise more money mainly because few donors noticed which ratio their letter offered.
a matching offer increases the number of people who give but leaves unchanged the amount of money that a mailing raises.
items.explanation: Any match raised more money than no match, so the offer of a match mattered. But tripling the match did no better than matching dollar for dollar, so how much the match added did not matter. Donors therefore reacted to whether a match was offered, not to its size, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The $1 match did as well as the larger ones, not better, and nothing in the text shows that larger matches discouraged anyone.

C.why_wrong: The text reports only that larger ratios did no better; it gives no evidence about whether donors noticed the ratio.

D.why_wrong: The text says letters offering a match raised more money per letter than letters offering none.

sources.what: Karlan and List 2007 (AER): direct mail to over 50,000 prior donors; the match offer increased both revenue per solicitation and response rate; larger match ratios ($3:$1, $2:$1) relative to $1:$1 had no additional impact

items.notes: Area: social science (economics). Hard S1 per 3.21: the comparison lies in two results that must be read together. Steps: (1) any match beats none, so a match matters; (2) larger ratios equal $1, so size does not, hence presence over size. Kept premises: A $1 as good as larger, C larger ratios no better, D matches change giving.

band7.why: Two results read together (any match beats none; larger ratios equal $1) give presence over size; A and C keep true pieces with an added mechanism, D a reversal. Strong band 6.

items.subtype: T1 elimination: isotope matches rule out local origin
items.passage: Researchers have long debated whether the agricultural fields of New Mexico’s Chaco Canyon could sustain the communities that built and occupied the canyon’s monumental great houses. Because a plant’s chemistry, including the ratio of two strontium isotopes, reflects that of the water that nourished it, geochemist Larry Benson and colleagues compared the chemistry of corncobs from one great house with that of water and soil samples from the canyon and from surrounding farmland. No cob matched the canyon samples: six matched an area at the base of the Chuska Mountains, 80 kilometers west, and one matched river floodplains 90 kilometers north, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the canyon’s soil and water could not have supported the growing of corn while the great houses were occupied.
corn grown near the Chuska Mountains was carried to the northern floodplains before being brought into the canyon.
residents of the great house regularly traveled to distant areas to plant and harvest the corn themselves.
some of the corn found at the great house had been grown in at least two regions far from the canyon.
items.explanation: Since a cob’s chemistry reflects where it grew, the absence of any match with the canyon’s samples rules out the canyon’s fields as the source of these cobs. The matches with areas 80 kilometers west and 90 kilometers north show that at least some of the great house’s corn came from two or more distant regions, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The cobs show only that this corn was not grown in the canyon; they do not show that no corn could have been grown there.

B.why_wrong: Six cobs matched the Chuska area and one matched the northern floodplains; nothing in the text indicates that corn from the Chuska area passed through the north on its way to the canyon.

C.why_wrong: The cobs’ chemistry shows where the corn grew, not who grew it; the text gives no information about whether the great house’s residents farmed the distant fields or obtained the corn from others.

sources.what: USGS Fact Sheet 2004-3035 on Benson et al. 2003: 87Sr/86Sr of Pueblo Bonito cobs compared with surface and soil waters; two canyon soil waters and one Fajada Wash sample fell in the cobs’ Sr range but trace-element ratios ruled those sites out, so no cob identified as grown in Chaco Canyon; six cobs probably grown in Newcomb-area fields at the base of the Chuskas (about 80 km west); one cob from the San Juan or Animas floodplains about 90 km north; maize transported over considerable distances

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. Great house not named (Pueblo Bonito is the subject noun of boundaries w1b2_14). Construction dates are background, rounded. Steps: (1) a plant’s chemistry (strontium ratio and trace elements) records where it grew, so no canyon match rules out the canyon; (2) two distant matches give at least two outside regions. Kept premises: A no canyon match (stretched to the canyon’s capacity), B both outside regions (route added), C distant fields (farmers assumed).

fixes: method stated as the cobs’ chemistry including the strontium ratio: by strontium alone two canyon soil waters and a Fajada Wash sample matched; trace elements excluded them (USGS fact sheet)
key D: ‘eaten’ (unsupported) now ‘found’, and trimmed from 23 to 21 words, no longer the clear longest option

band7.why: S4 elimination with two outside sources (at least two regions); A overreach from the null match, B a route added, C who grew it assumed; each keeps a true piece. Strong band 6.

items.subtype: T1 revision: radiocarbon dates overturn an age
items.passage: Crannogs, small artificial islands built in the lakes of Scotland and Ireland, were long thought by many archaeologists to date mostly from the Iron Age, which began roughly 2,800 years ago. After divers recovered Neolithic pottery from the water around several islets in Scotland’s Outer Hebrides, archaeologists Duncan Garrow and Fraser Sturt investigated the islets and obtained radiocarbon dates indicating that some of them were constructed between about 3640 and 3360 BCE. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: people in Scotland were building artificial islands thousands of years earlier than many archaeologists had assumed.
the islets in the Outer Hebrides were natural islands that Neolithic people visited but did not construct.
most of the crannogs found in Scotland and Ireland were built during the Neolithic period rather than during the Iron Age.
Neolithic pottery was traded from the Outer Hebrides to communities living on crannogs during the Iron Age.
items.explanation: Archaeologists had dated crannogs mostly to the Iron Age, about 2,800 years ago. Radiocarbon dates show that some islets in the Outer Hebrides were built more than 5,000 years ago, so people were constructing such islands long before the period archaeologists had assumed, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text says the dates show when some of the islets were built, so they were constructed, not merely visited.

C.why_wrong: The dates concern a few islets in the Outer Hebrides; they do not show when most crannogs in Scotland and Ireland were built.

D.why_wrong: The pottery and the building dates both point to the Neolithic; nothing in the text links the pottery to Iron Age communities.

sources.what: Garrow and Sturt 2019 (Antiquity): radiocarbon dates place four Outer Hebrides crannogs between 3640 and 3360 BC; many archaeologists had thought crannogs were Iron Age, about 2,800 years ago; divers had found Neolithic pottery around the islets

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology. S11: received view (Iron Age) plus counterevidence (Neolithic dates) gives the revision. Distractors: REV, EXT, MIX.

fixes: ‘four’ islets now ‘some’: the cited Smithsonian piece says five crannogs (six of eight timbers dated), other reports three or four

items.subtype: T3 consequence: technical constraint applied to early sound films
items.passage: In the late 1920s, when Hollywood studios began producing films with synchronized sound, the sensitive microphones then available captured the whirring of the camera’s motor along with the actors’ dialogue. To keep this mechanical noise off the soundtrack, technicians enclosed both the camera and its operator in a soundproof booth with a glass front, a structure so cumbersome and heavy that repositioning it during the filming of a scene was seldom practical. Consequently, many of the earliest sound films ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: were shot mostly outdoors, where the noise of the camera’s motor would not have been noticed.
had soundtracks on which the whirring of the camera could still be clearly heard.
consisted largely of scenes in which the camera stayed in a single position.
were made with cameras that were smaller and lighter than those used for silent films.
items.explanation: The booths that kept camera noise off the soundtrack were too large and heavy to move easily during filming. Cameras inside them would therefore tend to stay put for whole scenes, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says the problem was solved by enclosing the camera in a booth, not by moving filming outdoors.

B.why_wrong: The booths were built to keep the camera’s noise off the soundtrack.

D.why_wrong: The text says nothing about the size of the cameras themselves; what was large and heavy was the booth around them.

sources.what: 1956 account of the coming of the talkies: the camera made a noise, so technicians put it in a soundproof room with glass walls; the icebox weighed thousands of pounds and froze the camera, since much time and effort were involved in moving it; checked on the Wayback Machine copy (live host unreachable)

items.notes: Area: humanities (film history). S2: principle (camera noise must be isolated) plus case (heavy booth) gives the consequence (static camera). Distractors: CAUSE, REV, CMP.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: seasonal light principle applied to leaf retention
items.passage: In the deciduous forests of the eastern United States, shrubs in the understory are heavily shaded all summer but get far more sunlight once the trees overhead drop their leaves in autumn. Over three years, ecologist Jason Fridley and colleagues tracked native shrubs and nonnative ones introduced from Europe and East Asia, and they found that the nonnative shrubs kept their leaves and went on photosynthesizing nearly four weeks longer into autumn than the native ones did. This finding suggests that the nonnative shrubs ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: begin producing leaves earlier in spring than the native shrubs do, before the canopy trees have leafed out.
may make greater use than native shrubs do of the sunlight that reaches the understory in autumn.
are better able than native shrubs to photosynthesize in deep shade during the summer.
keep their leaves until the canopy trees grow new leaves the following spring.
items.explanation: Understory shrubs get much more sunlight once the canopy trees drop their leaves in autumn. Because the nonnative shrubs keep photosynthesizing about four weeks longer into autumn than native shrubs, they can use more of that late-season light, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text reports a difference in autumn; it gives no information about when either group of shrubs leafs out in spring.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about how well either group grows in summer shade; the difference it reports is in how long the shrubs keep their leaves in autumn.

D.why_wrong: Keeping leaves about four weeks longer into autumn does not mean keeping them through the winter.

sources.what: Fridley 2012 (Nature), Syracuse University release: three years of monitoring in eastern US deciduous forests; invasive shrubs (imported mainly from Europe, China and Japan) kept their leaves and kept photosynthesizing almost four weeks longer into the fall than their native cousins

items.notes: Area: natural science (forest ecology). S2: principle (understory light peaks after canopy leaf fall) plus case (nonnatives keep leaves four weeks longer) gives the consequence. Replaces the red snow claim (already an RS b7 subject). Distractors: MIX, CAUSE, EXT.

items.subtype: T5 status of evidence: rival cause for marks on bones
items.passage: In 2010, archaeologist Shannon McPherron and colleagues reported that two animal bones from Dikika, Ethiopia, more than 3.39 million years old, bore cut marks made by stone tools as hominins removed flesh—evidence that would predate the oldest known stone tools by roughly 800,000 years. Other researchers, including anthropologist Henry Bunn, countered that bones trampled by animals or scraped by sediment can bear grooves and scratches resembling cut marks. The marks on the Dikika bones, therefore, ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: may not show that hominins at Dikika were using stone tools to butcher animals.
show that the hominins at Dikika made stone tools that sediment later wore down.
were most likely made by animals trampling the bones rather than by stone tools.
suggest that the Dikika bones are considerably younger than 3.39 million years.
items.explanation: McPherron’s team read the marks as cuts made by stone tools, but critics point out that trampling and sediment can produce similar grooves. Since another process could have made the marks, they cannot by themselves establish that hominins at Dikika butchered animals with tools, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The text says sediment can scratch bones, not tools, and the critics’ point weakens rather than confirms the claim of tool use.

C.why_wrong: The critics show only that trampling could produce similar marks, not that it most likely did.

D.why_wrong: The debate concerns what made the marks, not the age of the bones, which the text gives as more than 3.39 million years.

sources.what: Earth magazine: McPherron’s 2010 Nature report of 3.39-million-year-old cut marks at Dikika challenged by a study (Bunn and colleagues) arguing the marks came from trampling or sediment grinding, which can cause deep grooves and fine scratches

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (paleoanthropology). S5: claim plus rival explanation gives a hedged conclusion. Distractors: MIX, EXT (most likely trampling), OUT.

items.subtype: T1 controlled comparison: random labels change ratings
items.passage: Neuroscientist Ulrich Kirk and colleagues, including Semir Zeki, investigated whether people judge art solely by its appearance. While monitoring participants’ brain activity, the researchers showed them a series of images and asked them to rate how aesthetically pleasing each one was. Before each image appeared, participants were told either that it came from an art gallery or that the researchers had generated it on a computer. In fact, all the images came from a single collection, and each label was assigned at random. Participants rated images labeled as gallery works more favorably than those labeled as computer-generated, and the difference corresponded to activity in brain regions involved in assigning value, suggesting that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: images produced on computers tend to be less pleasing to viewers than works that were made by human artists.
most people can reliably tell whether an image was made by an artist or generated on a computer.
brain activity, more than personal taste, determines which works of art people find pleasing.
people’s judgments of an artwork’s beauty may depend partly on what they believe about where it came from.
items.explanation: The images in both conditions came from the same set and the labels were assigned at random, so only the label differed. Because the gallery label raised ratings, beliefs about an image’s source appear to affect how beautiful it seems, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The images were the same in both conditions; only the label changed, so the study says nothing about images actually made on computers.

B.why_wrong: Participants were never asked to identify an image’s source, and the labels were assigned at random, so they could not have been telling real sources apart.

C.why_wrong: The text links the label’s effect to brain activity but does not compare the influence of brain activity with that of personal taste.

sources.what: Kirk, Skov, Hulme, Christensen, Zeki 2009 (NeuroImage): the same artworks randomly labelled as from a gallery or computer generated; aesthetic ratings significantly higher for gallery context; the modulation correlated with medial orbitofrontal and prefrontal activity

items.notes: Area: humanities (art, aesthetics) with psychology. S1: groups differ only in label; outcome differs, so the label affects judgment. Distractors: REV (confound), OUT, EXT.

items.subtype: T1 two cases with opposite outcomes give a conditional
items.passage: The nonvenomous scarlet kingsnake has red, black, and yellow rings that resemble those of the venomous eastern coral snake. To determine whether this resemblance protects the kingsnake, biologists David Pfennig, William Harcombe, and Karin Pfennig placed clay imitations of snakes—some ringed like kingsnakes, others striped or plain brown—in the Carolinas, both within the coral snake’s range and in areas farther north where coral snakes do not live. Within the coral snake’s range, predators attacked ringed imitations far less often than the others, but outside it they attacked ringed imitations about as often as the others. The researchers therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: predators in areas without coral snakes cannot distinguish the colors of the ringed replicas from those of the plain ones.
kingsnakes living outside the coral snake’s range have evolved coloring that differs from that of coral snakes.
the kingsnake’s rings protect it from predators only where predators are likely to encounter coral snakes.
ringed coloring protects snakes from predators everywhere but does so more strongly where coral snakes live.
items.explanation: Ringed replicas were attacked less only inside the coral snake’s range; elsewhere they fared no better than plain or striped ones. The protection therefore depends on coral snakes being present, presumably because predators there learn to avoid ringed snakes, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text gives no information about predators’ color vision; it explains the difference by whether coral snakes live in the area.

B.why_wrong: The study used replicas with identical rings in both areas; it did not examine the coloring of real kingsnakes.

D.why_wrong: Outside the coral snake’s range ringed replicas were attacked about as often as the others, so the rings gave no protection there.

sources.what: ScienceDaily on Pfennig, Harcombe, Pfennig 2001 (Nature): plasticine models of scarlet kingsnakes with striped or plain brown controls, placed within the coral snake’s range in the Carolinas and north of it in central North Carolina; ringed models readily attacked only where no coral snakes lived (about 50 percent vs about 6 percent)

items.notes: Area: natural science (ecology, mimicry). Replicas were plasticine, given as clay. S7: two places with opposite outcomes give 'only where'. Distractors: CAUSE, OUT, EXT.

fixes: source swapped: nature.com link redirects to a login; ScienceDaily release states the design and the result

items.subtype: T1 co-occurrence: two parallel reductions point to a link
items.passage: Seagrass meadows frequently grow in the shallow waters immediately adjacent to coral reefs. Marine ecologist Joleah Lamb and colleagues sampled seawater around small islands in the Indonesian archipelago and found that where seagrass was present, the relative abundance of potentially pathogenic bacteria—those capable of causing disease in humans, fish, and invertebrates—was approximately half of what it was at sites with no seagrass. Surveying more than 8,000 reef-building corals, the team also determined that corals next to seagrass meadows had half as much disease as corals at comparable sites with no seagrass nearby. Together, these findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: corals that grow beside seagrass meadows are naturally more resistant to disease than other corals are.
seagrass meadows may help protect nearby corals by reducing the number of harmful bacteria in the water.
the bacteria that cause disease in corals are carried to reefs mainly from seagrass meadows.
seagrass meadows reduce disease in corals but have little effect on bacteria that harm fish or invertebrates.
items.explanation: Where seagrass grows, the water holds about half as many potentially harmful bacteria, and corals next to seagrass have about half as much disease. These matching patterns suggest that seagrass lowers corals’ exposure to disease-causing bacteria, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text links the lower disease levels to the water around seagrass, which held fewer harmful bacteria, not to any trait of the corals themselves.

C.why_wrong: The water near seagrass held fewer harmful bacteria, not more.

D.why_wrong: The text says the reduced bacteria include those that cause disease in fish and invertebrates.

sources.what: Lamb et al. 2017 (Science): where seagrass meadows were present there was a 50% reduction in the relative abundance of potential bacterial pathogens of humans, fishes and invertebrates; surveys of more than 8,000 reef-building corals next to seagrass showed twofold reductions in disease

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine ecology). S8: two observations line up (fewer pathogens, less coral disease), so seagrass may be linked to coral health. Distractors: CAUSE, REV, MIX.

items.subtype: T1 elimination: signal geometry rules out a distant source
items.passage: For years, astronomers at Australia’s Parkes radio telescope intermittently recorded brief bursts of radio waves that they named perytons. In principle, such bursts could originate either from an astronomical object far out in space or from a terrestrial source on or near Earth. The telescope’s receiver collects signals through 13 separate beams, each aimed at a slightly different part of the sky, so a signal from a single distant point would show up in only one beam or a few neighboring ones. Perytons, however, appeared approximately equally strong in all 13 beams simultaneously. The astronomers therefore concluded that perytons ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: most likely originated on or near Earth rather than in distant space.
came from a distant object that crossed all 13 patches of sky within a few seconds.
were produced by a fault in one of the receiver’s 13 beams.
came from many separate objects in space that each happened to emit a burst at once.
items.explanation: A burst from a distant point in the sky would show up in only one beam or a few neighboring ones. Since perytons were equally strong in all 13 beams, the distant-source explanation does not fit, leaving a source on or near Earth, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The bursts were brief and appeared in all 13 beams at once, not one beam after another as a moving object would.

C.why_wrong: A fault in one beam would affect that beam only, but perytons appeared equally in all 13 beams.

D.why_wrong: Nothing in the text suggests many objects bursting at the same moment; the simpler conclusion the evidence supports is a nearby source.

sources.what: Sky & Telescope on Petroff et al. 2015: Parkes watches the sky along 13 beams; unlike a point-like astrophysical source, perytons appear equally bright in all 13 beams; traced to microwave ovens on site

items.notes: Area: natural science (astronomy). S4: two possible origins; the all-beam pattern rules out a distant point, leaving a nearby source (later traced to microwave ovens). Distractors: MIX, MIX, EXT.

items.subtype: T6 design reveals purpose
items.passage: In 1801, William Little and William Smith published The Easy Instructor, a collection of hymns intended for singing schools—community classes where many Americans learned church music. In this book, every note was printed in one of four distinctive shapes: a triangle, a circle, a square, or a diamond. Each shape corresponded to one of the syllables that singers traditionally used to identify the notes of a scale. Little and Smith most likely designed this system because ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: printing notes in four different shapes cost less than printing them in the usual round form.
most singers in these schools already knew how to read notes printed in the usual round form.
the shapes made it easier for singers without musical training to recognize the notes of a scale.
the shapes allowed composers to write music that used more than four different notes.
items.explanation: The book was made for singing schools where ordinary people learned to sing, and each shape matched a syllable naming a note of the scale. Giving every note a shape that singers could recognize at a glance would help untrained singers read music, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The text says nothing about printing costs.

B.why_wrong: If singers could already read ordinary notes, the shapes would not be needed; the book’s title and purpose point to learners.

D.why_wrong: The text says the shapes matched four syllables; it says nothing about letting composers use more notes.

sources.what: Shape note: introduced in The Easy Instructor (1801) by William Little and William Smith; fa, sol, la, mi each given a distinct shape; designed to facilitate congregational and community singing in singing schools

items.notes: Area: humanities (music history). S9: design (shapes tied to syllables) reveals purpose (help learners read music). Distractors: OUT, REV, OUT.

items.subtype: T1 controlled comparison: one variable changed
items.passage: Mussels attach themselves to rocks and to one another with byssal threads, remarkably strong fibers that they make. The threads keep them from being swept away by waves. As the ocean takes in carbon dioxide from the atmosphere, its water is gradually becoming more acidic. Researchers Michael O’Donnell, Matthew George, and Emily Carrington wanted to determine whether this change could affect the threads. They raised mussels in laboratory tanks with different amounts of carbon dioxide. Threads made in the tanks with the most carbon dioxide were weaker and less stretchy than threads made in normal seawater. The mussels’ shells and bodies, however, grew normally. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: mussels in more acidic water grow smaller shells in order to save energy for making threads.
high levels of carbon dioxide harm most kinds of ocean animals more than they harm mussels.
mussels make more threads when the water around them contains more carbon dioxide.
as ocean water becomes more acidic, waves may tear mussels loose from rocks more easily.
items.explanation: Mussels rely on their threads to stay attached against the waves, and threads made in water with more carbon dioxide were weaker. As the ocean grows more acidic, mussels may therefore be pulled loose more easily, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The text says the mussels’ shells and bodies grew normally.

B.why_wrong: The study examined only mussels, so it cannot show how other ocean animals are affected.

C.why_wrong: The text reports how strong the threads were, not how many were made.

sources.what: OA-ICC repost of the abstract, O’Donnell, George, Carrington 2013 (Nature Climate Change): byssal threads secreted under elevated pCO2 were weaker and less extensible, whereas shell and tissue growth were unaffected

items.notes: Area: natural science (marine biology). S1 easy: tanks differ only in carbon dioxide; threads weaker. Distractors: REV, CMP, VAR.

fixes: source swapped: the UW page gives only the title; the OA-ICC repost of the abstract states weaker, less stretchy threads and normal shell and tissue growth

items.subtype: T4 X but not Y: one ability kept, one lost
items.passage: During courtship, a male Anna’s hummingbird climbs about 30 meters into the air and then dives past a female, making a loud chirp at the bottom of the dive. Scientists long debated whether hummingbirds create this sound vocally or mechanically, with their feathers. Biologists Christopher Clark and Teresa Feo filmed the dives with high-speed cameras and discovered that the chirp occurs precisely as the male spreads his tail. They then removed or trimmed the two outermost tail feathers of some males. These birds could still fly, but they could no longer make the characteristic chirp. This suggests that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: males with trimmed tail feathers cannot dive steeply enough to attract a female’s attention.
the chirp is produced by the two outer tail feathers rather than by the bird’s voice.
the chirp warns other male hummingbirds to stay away from the female.
female hummingbirds prefer males whose tail feathers are longer than those of other males.
items.explanation: Removing or trimming the two outer tail feathers stopped the chirp, but the birds could still fly, so the loss of the sound was not caused by an inability to fly. The feathers themselves must make the chirp, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says the birds could still fly; it does not say that their dives changed.

C.why_wrong: The text says nothing about what the chirp communicates to other males.

D.why_wrong: The study tested how the sound is made, not which males females prefer.

sources.what: Clark and Feo 2008 (Proc R Soc B), UC Berkeley release: males ascend 100 feet or more; chirp coincides with a 60 ms spreading of the tail; sound made by the inner vanes of the two outer tail feathers; males missing those feathers or with inner vanes trimmed were unable to make dive sounds; birds can fly without them

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior). S6: flight kept, chirp lost, so the feathers make the sound. Distractors: REV, OUT, CMP.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: two measures applied to the route by which newcomers had gained power
items.passage: In medieval Venice, a contract known as the colleganza enabled merchants with little capital of their own to undertake trading voyages financed by investors who remained at home, the two parties dividing any profits. Economists Diego Puga and Daniel Trefler argue that such contracts enriched a broad group of newcomers, who then used their wealth to press for a larger share of political authority. After 1297, however, a group of exceptionally wealthy merchants made membership in Venice’s parliament hereditary and erected barriers to participation in the most lucrative branches of long-distance commerce. Taken together, these measures most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: barred newly rich merchants from parliament but left them free to compete with established families for the profits of long-distance trade.
made established families more dependent on newcomers, whose investments through the colleganza were needed to finance the most profitable voyages.
blocked outsiders’ path to political power directly while also cutting off the trade wealth that had fueled earlier challenges.
reduced the overall volume of Venice’s long-distance trade by discouraging investors from financing voyages abroad.
items.explanation: New merchants had gained political power by first growing rich through long-distance trade. Making parliament hereditary shut them out of power directly, and the barriers to the most lucrative trade cut off the wealth that had made their earlier rise possible, as C says.

A.why_wrong: Hereditary membership did bar newcomers from parliament, but the text says the same merchants also erected barriers to the most lucrative trade, so newcomers were not left free to compete for its profits.

B.why_wrong: The measures were meant to shut newcomers out; nothing suggests the established families came to depend on them, and the text never says the elite needed newcomers' money.

D.why_wrong: The text says who could take part in the most lucrative trade, not that the total amount of trade fell or that investors stopped financing voyages.

sources.what: Puga and Trefler: long-distance trade enriched a broad group of merchants who pushed for constraints on the executive; colleganza mobilized capital for risky long-distance trade; after 1297 a small group of wealthy merchants made parliamentary participation hereditary and erected barriers to participation in the most lucrative aspects of long-distance trade

items.notes: Area: history (economic history). Steps: (1) newcomers rose by turning trade wealth into political power; (2) the two measures close the political door and the economic route that fed it. Kept premises: A keeps the political half, B keeps the colleganza, D keeps the trade barriers.

fixes: removed 'small' before 'group of exceptionally wealthy merchants' (the NBER abstract says 'a group of extraordinarily rich merchants')

band7.why: Two linked steps (trade wealth fed the newcomers' push for power; the measures close the political door and the wealth route) and all three distractors keep a true piece, but options average about 18 words (gate 20), only one REV or MIX, and the premise sits one sentence back: a strong band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: proposed inheritance rule applied to the offspring of tuskless females
items.passage: During Mozambique’s civil war (1977–1992), ivory poaching eliminated most of the elephants in Gorongosa National Park, and the proportion of females lacking tusks increased from about 18.5 percent to about 51 percent. Evolutionary biologist Shane Campbell-Staton and colleagues documented no tuskless males in the park and proposed that tusklessness results from a dominant mutation on the X chromosome that is lethal to males before birth. Males inherit their single X chromosome from their mothers, whereas females inherit one X chromosome from each parent. If the researchers’ proposal is correct, tuskless females would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: give birth to noticeably fewer male calves than female calves.
pass tusklessness to every daughter, since each daughter inherits an X chromosome from her mother.
have inherited the mutation from their fathers, who carried it without being harmed by it.
disappear from the park within a few generations, since every male that inherits the mutation dies.
items.explanation: Because the mutation kills males, no father can carry it, so a tuskless female has it on only one of her two X chromosomes. About half of her sons would inherit that X and die before birth, while her daughters would survive whether or not they inherit it, so she would bear fewer sons than daughters, as A says.

B.why_wrong: A tuskless female has the mutation on only one of her two X chromosomes, so each daughter has about an even chance of inheriting it, not a certainty.

C.why_wrong: A male that inherited the mutation would die before birth, so no living father could carry it; tuskless females must have inherited it from their mothers.

D.why_wrong: Males with the mutation die, but tuskless females survive and pass it to about half their daughters, so nothing in the proposal implies that tuskless females would vanish within a few generations.

sources.what: Princeton release on Campbell-Staton et al., Science 2021: Mozambican Civil War 1977 to 1992; tuskless females rose from 18.5% to 50.9%; zero tuskless males recorded; trait consistent with X-linked inheritance lethal to males; tuskless mothers' offspring 65.7% female

items.notes: Area: natural science (evolution, genetics). Steps: (1) a male-lethal mutation cannot come from a father, so tuskless females carry one copy; (2) half their sons inherit it and die, skewing births toward daughters (the source reports 65.7% female offspring, left out so the item asks for it). The mechanism is stated as the team's proposal, as the source does.

band7.why: B and C need the full chain (no carrier fathers, so tuskless mothers carry one copy), but the key itself follows from male lethality before birth in about one step; options about 13 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a critic's claim about one translator applied to readers of two authors
items.passage: For decades, many English-speaking readers knew the great nineteenth-century Russian novelists chiefly through the work of one translator, Constance Garnett, who worked fast and produced 71 volumes of Russian literature, among them novels by both Leo Tolstoy and Fyodor Dostoevsky. Translation scholar Rachel May has argued that Garnett’s versions homogenized the styles of the authors she translated, smoothing away the idiosyncrasies of narrative voice and dialogue that distinguish one writer’s prose from another’s. If May is right, then readers who knew both of these novelists only through Garnett’s translations would likely have ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: regarded the two novelists’ plots and characters as largely interchangeable with each other.
noticed the sameness of style and attributed it to Garnett rather than to the novelists themselves.
found Garnett’s versions of Dostoevsky more faithful to the originals than her versions of Tolstoy.
perceived the two novelists’ prose as more alike than it is in Russian.
items.explanation: May argues that Garnett gave the authors she translated one smoothed style, erasing what distinguished their voices and dialogue. Readers who met both Tolstoy and Dostoevsky only in her versions were therefore reading one style twice and would likely have found the two writers’ prose more similar than it really is, as D says.

A.why_wrong: May’s claim concerns style, the voice and dialogue of the prose; it gives no reason to think readers would confuse the novelists’ plots and characters.

B.why_wrong: Readers who knew the novels only in Garnett’s English had nothing to compare her versions with, so the text gives no basis for thinking they would trace the sameness to her.

C.why_wrong: The text never compares how faithful Garnett was to one author rather than the other; May’s claim applies to the authors she translated generally.

sources.what: Constance Garnett translated 71 volumes of Russian literature and worked quickly; Rachel May criticized her stylistic homogenizing, erasing idiosyncrasies of narrative voice and dialogue that different authors possessed; Brodsky: English readers can barely tell Tolstoy from Dostoevsky because they are reading Garnett

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature, translation). Steps: (1) one translator, one homogenized style; (2) both novelists read only through her, so their styles seem alike. Kept premises: A stretches style to plot, B keeps the sameness, C keeps the two authors. Brodsky's remark left out so the key is inferred, not quoted.

band7.why: Two steps (one translator, one smoothed style; both authors read only through her); A and B partly right, key paraphrased; options about 15 words and one REV: band 6.

items.subtype: T2 purpose of a design feature, given a stated principle about norms
items.passage: Telling people how their behavior compares with the norm can backfire: such comparative information may draw those whose conduct is better than average back toward the average. Investigating one potential remedy, psychologist P. Wesley Schultz and colleagues gave households in San Marcos, California, written feedback comparing each home’s recent electricity consumption with the neighborhood average; some feedback sheets also carried an emoticon, a frowning face if the household had consumed more energy than average and a smiling face if it had consumed less. For households with below-average consumption, the smiling face was most likely intended to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: shame them into cutting their energy use still further below the average for their neighborhood.
counter the pull of the average by signaling approval of their already low energy use.
show them how far below the neighborhood average their energy use had fallen.
encourage households that used more energy than average to imitate their thriftier neighbors.
items.explanation: The text says a comparison with the norm can draw households that are doing better than average back toward it, so low-use households told the average risk using more. A smile signals approval, so it tells those households that their low use is good, which works against that pull, as B says.

A.why_wrong: A smile signals approval, not shame; it was attached for households already below the average, to keep their use low rather than to push it lower.

C.why_wrong: The comparison with the neighborhood average already showed each household where it stood; the face was added to that comparison, so its purpose was something else.

D.why_wrong: High-use households received a frown on their own sheets; a smile on a low-use household’s sheet was meant for that household.

sources.what: Schultz 2007 (ScienceDaily): households in San Marcos got their actual energy use and how it compared with the average; frugal households given only the data used more; an emoticon was attached, a smiley face for below-average and a frown for above-average households; praised frugal households did not increase use

items.notes: Area: social science (psychology). Steps: (1) the norm pulls low users up toward the average; (2) a smile signals approval and so counters that pull. Kept premises: A keeps conservation, C keeps the comparison, D keeps the frown condition. The result (smile households did not increase) left out so the item asks for the purpose.

band7.why: Needed premise is sentence 1, two sentences from the blank, and C is true-but-not-the-step, but A (shame) and D (wrong group) each fall to one fact; options about 15 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T3 consequence: a finding about what predicts word length applied to two equally frequent words
items.passage: In the 1930s, linguist George Kingsley Zipf observed that frequently used words tend to be short, and for decades word length was attributed principally to frequency of use. Analyzing texts in numerous languages, cognitive scientists Steven Piantadosi, Harry Tily, and Edward Gibson found that a word’s length is better predicted by its average information content, which is low when the surrounding context typically makes the word easy to anticipate, than by its frequency. If two words in a language occurred equally often but one usually appeared in contexts where it was highly predictable, that word would most likely ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: be about as long as the other word, since the two words are used equally often.
be longer than the other word, which would help listeners tell the two apart.
be the shorter of the two, since it typically carries less information where it occurs.
gradually be replaced by a less predictable word that conveys more information.
items.explanation: A word that is easy to guess from its context has low information content, and Piantadosi’s team found that low information content goes with short words. Since frequency is the same for both words, the easily predicted one should be the shorter, as C says.

A.recipe: older view in place of the finding (MIX)
A.why_wrong: Equal frequency would predict equal length only on the older frequency explanation; the team found information content a better predictor, and the two words differ in that.

B.why_wrong: Low information content goes with shorter words, not longer ones, and the text says nothing about length helping listeners tell words apart.

D.why_wrong: The text is about which words are short, not about words being replaced over time.

sources.what: Piantadosi, Tily and Gibson, PNAS 2011: across languages, average information content is a much better predictor of word length than frequency, challenging Zipf's frequency account

items.notes: Area: social science (linguistics). Steps: (1) easy to predict means low information content; (2) low information content means a shorter word, with frequency held equal so Zipf's account cannot decide. Kept premises: A keeps frequency (the old view), B keeps length, D keeps information content.

band7.why: Key needs the aside defining information content plus the finding; A is a strong partly-right (the old frequency view), B and D fall quickly; options about 15 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T6 function of a behavior, from a perception experiment
items.passage: As a large animal approaches, a rattlesnake shakes its rattle progressively faster until, at a certain point, it abruptly switches to a considerably higher rate of roughly 60 to 100 shakes per second. To investigate how human listeners perceive this escalating display, neurobiologist Boris Chagnaud and his colleagues moved participants through a virtual grassland toward a concealed snake whose rattling followed the same pattern; when the rate suddenly jumped, participants judged the snake to be nearer than it actually was. This observation suggests that the abrupt switch most likely serves to ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: make an approaching animal stop farther from the snake than it otherwise would.
convince an approaching animal that the snake is larger than it actually is.
signal that the snake is about to strike, regardless of how far away the intruder is.
make the rattle audible to animals that are still too far away to hear the slower rattling.
items.explanation: When the rate jumped, listeners believed the snake was closer than it really was. An animal that thinks it is already near the snake would halt sooner, leaving more distance between them, so the switch likely serves to keep intruders farther away, as A says.

B.why_wrong: Participants misjudged how far away the snake was, not how big it was.

C.why_wrong: The switch comes as the intruder gets close and changes how near the snake seems; the text gives no sign that it announces a strike, let alone at any distance.

D.why_wrong: The high rate begins only after the intruder has come close; animals still far away hear the slower rattling, so the switch is not aimed at them.

sources.what: Forsthofer, Chagnaud et al., Current Biology 2021: rattling rate increases as threats approach, then abruptly switches to 60 to 100 Hz; in a virtual reality grassland the sudden increase made participants underestimate their distance to the snake, creating a distance safety margin

items.notes: Area: natural science (animal behavior, perception). Steps: (1) the jump makes the snake seem closer; (2) an intruder who thinks it is close stops sooner, keeping a margin. Note: an official Command of Evidence item studies rattlesnake stress with a companion; this subject (rattle frequency and distance perception) is different.

fixes: researchers trimmed to 'neurobiologist Boris Chagnaud and his colleagues' (the cited page names only Chagnaud)

band7.why: Two steps (judged nearer, so the intruder halts sooner); B and D keep true pieces, key paraphrased away from the passage; options about 15 words: band 6.

items.subtype: T2 motive inferred from the timing of an author's decision
items.passage: Like most of Charles Dickens’s novels, Martin Chuzzlewit was published in monthly installments, appearing between 1843 and 1844, and Dickens was still writing the novel while its installments were going on sale. Sales of the early installments were noticeably lower than those of his previous novels. Then, at the end of the fifth installment, the novel’s young protagonist abruptly announces that he will go to the United States, and later installments follow him there through a lengthy succession of unfamiliar American settings and characters. The timing of this development suggests that Dickens ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: had planned from the start to move the story to the United States after its fifth installment.
had run out of ideas for the novel’s English scenes, since he was still writing the novel while its installments were going on sale.
was responding to requests from readers of his earlier novels for stories set outside England.
took advantage of serial publication to try to attract more buyers to a slow-selling novel.
items.explanation: Because Dickens was still writing the novel as its installments went on sale, he could change course after seeing how the first parts sold. The abrupt move to America came after sales of the early installments fell short of his earlier novels, so it was likely an attempt to draw more buyers, as D says.

A.why_wrong: The change is described as abrupt and came after weak early sales, while Dickens was still writing the novel, which points to a decision made along the way, not a plan from the start.

B.why_wrong: Dickens was indeed writing as the installments appeared, but that was true from the start; what the change followed was weak sales, and the text never suggests he had run short of ideas.

C.why_wrong: The text mentions only the low sales of this novel’s early installments; it never mentions any requests from readers of his earlier novels.

sources.what: Martin Chuzzlewit: serialized 1843 to 1844; early sales of the monthly parts were lower than those of previous works, so Dickens changed the plot to send the title character to the United States

items.notes: Area: humanities (literature, publishing history). Steps: (1) writing month by month let him change course; (2) the change followed weak sales, so it aimed to lift them. Sales figures left out (only one secondary page gives 20,000). His 1842 American tour not mentioned and no option uses it, so no second motive is defensible. Reviewer: the source (Slater note on the cited page) puts Martin's sudden announcement at the end of Part V, so the passage now says the fifth installment; the writing-schedule clause is cut back to what the page implies (he changed the plot after weak early sales); B, a plain off-topic claim, is now a rival cause that keeps the schedule premise.

fixes: 'in the sixth installment' changed to 'at the end of the fifth installment', where the cited page's Slater note puts Martin's sudden announcement

'wrote each installment only shortly before it went on sale' softened to 'was still writing the novel while its installments were going on sale' (implied by the page: he changed the plot after weak early sales)
B (plain off-topic) replaced by a partly-right rival cause that keeps the writing-schedule premise; A reworded to the fifth installment

band7.why: Two steps (still writing, so able to change course; change followed weak sales); after the fix A and B keep true premises, but C is a plain rival motive and options average about 17 words: band 6.

items.subtype: Timeline rejects a premise: the horse lineage spread a thousand years after the expansion
items.passage: Around 3000 BCE, herders of the Yamnaya culture expanded from the steppes north of the Black Sea into much of Europe, a migration that many archaeologists have attributed to horseback riding and linked to the dispersal of Indo-European languages. Analyzing the genomes of 273 ancient horses, Pablo Librado, Ludovic Orlando, and colleagues traced all modern domestic horses to a lineage from the steppe’s lower Volga-Don region; apart from two individuals found on the steppe, no sampled horse older than about 2200 BCE belonged to it, and the lineage replaced most other horse populations across Eurasia only from about 2000 BCE, together with chariots. The team therefore concluded that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: Yamnaya herders brought into Europe the horses that later replaced Eurasia’s other horse populations.
the Yamnaya expansion into Europe probably did not rely on horses of the lineage that spread later.
Indo-European languages could not have reached Europe before domestic horses spread there around 2000 BCE.
chariots were developed in Europe and later carried east to the lower Volga-Don region.
items.explanation: The Yamnaya reached Europe around 3000 BCE, but apart from two steppe horses, no sampled horse older than about 2200 BCE belonged to the lineage of modern domestic horses, which spread across Eurasia only from about 2000 BCE. Horses of that lineage therefore could not have carried the expansion into Europe a thousand years earlier, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The lineage is absent from sampled horses older than about 2200 BCE apart from two on the steppe, and it spread across Eurasia only from about 2000 BCE, about a thousand years after the Yamnaya reached Europe, so the herders could not have brought those horses with them.

C.why_wrong: The finding separates the expansion from this horse lineage; it does not move the expansion itself, which the text dates to around 3000 BCE, and says nothing about when languages arrived.

D.why_wrong: The text places the lineage’s origin in the lower Volga-Don region and says it spread outward with chariots, not that chariots came from Europe.

sources.what: Librado et al., Nature 2021: 273 ancient horse genomes; modern domestic horses (DOM2) originated in the lower Volga-Don region and replaced most other populations from about 2000 BC, together with spoke-wheeled chariots; this rejects the association between horseback riding and the Yamnaya expansion into Europe around 3000 BC; genetic continuity with DOM2 rejected for horses older than about 2200 BC, except two late Yamnaya horses from Turganik east of the lower Volga-Don

items.notes: Area: history and archaeology (ancient DNA). Steps: (1) compare dates: expansion about 3000 BCE, horse lineage spreads about 2000 BCE; (2) so the lineage cannot have carried the expansion. Kept premises: A keeps the replacement, C keeps the languages and 2000 BCE, D keeps chariots and the Volga-Don.

band7.why: Negative key, three dates with an exception the key must honour, and every distractor keeps a true piece (A rescues the received view, D reverses the direction), but one date comparison settles it and options average about 15 words: a strong band 6.

items.subtype: X but not Y: tariffed and untariffed goods rose alike, so a washer-only estimate of the cost falls short
items.passage: In 2012, the United States imposed antidumping duties on washing machines from South Korea and Mexico, and in 2016 on those from China, yet washer prices barely changed, partly because manufacturers relocated production to other countries. In 2018, by contrast, tariffs covered washers from virtually all exporting countries. Economists Aaron Flaaen, Ali Hortaçsu, and Felix Tintelnot found that washer prices subsequently rose by nearly 12 percent and that the prices of clothes dryers, which were not taxed but are often bought along with washers, increased by about the same amount. These findings suggest that an estimate of the tariffs’ cost to US consumers calculated only from washer prices would ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: be accurate, since the tariffs applied only to washers and not to dryers.
understate that cost, since manufacturers again moved production to countries that the tariffs did not cover.
understate that cost, since consumers also paid more for a product that the tariffs did not cover.
overstate that cost, since washer prices had barely changed after the earlier duties on particular countries.
items.explanation: Dryers were not taxed, yet their prices rose about as much as washer prices did, and the two are often bought together, so the tariffs raised what consumers paid for dryers as well. An estimate calculated only from washer prices would leave that extra cost out and so would come in too low, as C says.

A.why_wrong: The tariffs did cover only washers, but dryer prices rose by about as much as washer prices; an estimate that ignored dryers would miss that increase, so it would not be accurate.

B.why_wrong: Moving production abroad is what happened after the earlier duties; the 2018 tariffs covered washers from virtually all exporting countries and washer prices rose, and a move abroad would not make a washer-only estimate too low in any case.

D.why_wrong: What happened after the earlier duties says nothing about the size of the 2018 cost, and the rise in dryer prices means a washer-only estimate would leave costs out, not count too much.

sources.what: Flaaen, Hortacsu and Tintelnot, AER 2020, abstract: 2012 and 2016 antidumping duties on South Korea and China were accompanied by minor price movements and production relocation; 2018 tariffs on nearly all source countries raised washer prices nearly 12 percent; dryer prices, not subject to tariffs, rose by an equivalent amount; factoring in dryer prices, the tariffs imply a tariff elasticity of consumer prices above one (so a washer-only figure falls short). Washers and dryers bought together: general knowledge, a smaller detail.

items.notes: Area: social science (economics). S6: washers taxed, dryers not, prices rose alike. Reviewer hardened it (the old key was close to a summary of the two stated facts): the lead-in now asks what a washer-only estimate of the cost would do. Steps: (1) the untaxed dryer rose with the taxed washer and the two are bought together, so the tariffs raised dryer prices too; (2) an estimate from washer prices leaves that out and comes in low. B and C share the phrase 'not cover' with different referents (countries, a product); A keeps the tariff's scope; D keeps the earlier episode. No option says washer prices rose less than the tariff, which the passage cannot rule out. The source's own estimate accounts for dryer prices.

fixes: hardened: lead-in now asks what a washer-only estimate of the 2018 cost would do, so the key needs two linked steps and is no longer a summary
options rebuilt as a near-miss set: B and C share 'not cover' with different referents, A keeps the tariff scope, D the earlier episode; old A (shared parts) and old B dropped
added that dryers are often bought together with washers so the dryer rise reads as a tariff effect
review.safety_fix: safety solve noted the 2012 duties covered South Korea and Mexico, not South Korea and China; passage and option D corrected (2016 duties covered China)

band7.why: After hardening the key needs two linked steps (dryer rise is a tariff cost; a washer-only estimate omits it) and all three distractors are partly right (2 MIX), but the dryer premise is the sentence before the blank and options average about 16 words: a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Received view plus counterevidence leads to a revised account of the within-country link
items.passage: Within any single country, individuals with higher incomes tend to report greater life satisfaction than those with lower incomes. In the 1970s, however, economist Richard Easterlin reported that wealthier countries were not reliably happier on average than poorer ones, a pattern frequently interpreted to mean that people judge their incomes primarily against those of the people around them. Reassessing the question with decades of survey data from many countries, economists Betsey Stevenson and Justin Wolfers found that average life satisfaction rises with national income at about the same rate at which individual satisfaction rises with individual income within a country. These findings suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: the link between income and life satisfaction within a country probably does not come mainly from comparisons with other people’s incomes.
people’s life satisfaction is not affected at all by how their incomes compare with those of other people.
residents of wealthier countries are more satisfied than residents of poorer countries chiefly because they compare themselves with people in poorer countries.
a person’s life satisfaction depends more on the average income of his or her country than on his or her own income.
items.explanation: If people judged their incomes only against those around them, a rise in a whole country’s income would leave everyone’s relative position unchanged, so richer countries would be no happier. Stevenson and Wolfers found instead that average satisfaction rises with national income about as fast as individual satisfaction rises with individual income. That suggests that the amount people earn, not mainly how it ranks, explains why richer people within a country are more satisfied, as A says.

B.why_wrong: The findings weaken the view that comparisons are the main reason income matters, but rates that are only about the same cannot show that comparisons play no part at all.

C.why_wrong: The text gives no evidence that people compare themselves with residents of other countries; the findings point to income itself, not to a different kind of comparison.

D.why_wrong: The findings say national income and individual income go with satisfaction at about the same rate, not that a country’s average income matters more than a person’s own.

sources.what: Stevenson and Wolfers, NBER w14282 (2008), Reassessing the Easterlin Paradox: clear positive link between average subjective well-being and GDP per capita; the cross-country relationship resembles the within-country income and happiness relationship; a clear role for absolute income and a more limited role for relative income comparisons

items.notes: Area: social science (economics, psychology). Reviewer hardened it: the doubt frame ('calling into question the assumption that') let three stated or supported claims fall at once, so the frame is now positive. Steps: (1) a comparison account predicts no rise in average satisfaction when a whole country grows richer, since no one's rank changes; (2) the national rise matches the individual one, so the within-country link of sentence 1 is not mainly about comparison. Key hedged to the source ('a more limited role for relative income comparisons'). B overstates the key, C rescues the comparison view with another reference group, D misreads 'about the same rate'. No option mentions a satiation point, which the passage does not address.

fixes: hardened: doubt frame replaced by a positive frame; key is now a hedged revision of the within-country link (source: 'a more limited role for relative income comparisons')
distractors rebuilt as partly right: overreach of the key (no effect), rescue of the comparison view (other countries), wrong level (country income over own income)
plain words: 'evaluate their incomes' to 'judge their incomes' (other long words kept for the tier's register gate)

band7.why: After hardening: negative hedged key, premise two sentences back, three partly-right distractors (EXT, REV rescue, MIX), options about 20 words; it meets several band-7 signals, but the chain is the one the passage sets up step by step, so judged a strong band 6.

items.subtype: Opposite individual outcomes lead to a 'depends on' conclusion
items.passage: Whole-grain sourdough bread is widely presumed to be nutritionally superior to industrially produced white bread. In a randomized trial led by Tal Korem, Eran Elinav, and Eran Segal, a group of healthy adults ate each type of bread for a week, one after the other. Averaged across participants, the two breads produced no significantly different effects on blood sugar or other clinical indicators; individual responses, however, varied considerably, and which bread produced the smaller rise in blood sugar for a given person could be predicted from measurements of that person’s gut bacteria taken before the trial. These results suggest that ______
items.stem: Which choice most logically completes the text?
options: sourdough bread lowers blood sugar in most people, although the effect is too small to detect in an average.
the effect of sourdough on a person’s blood sugar may depend partly on that person’s gut bacteria.
the kind of bread a person eats has little effect on that person’s blood sugar.
eating a single kind of bread for a week can change which bacteria live in a person’s gut.
items.explanation: On average the breads did not differ, yet for each person one bread produced a lower rise in blood sugar, and which one could be predicted from the person’s gut bacteria. So whether sourdough helps depends on the person, and the bacteria appear to be part of what decides it, as B says.

A.why_wrong: The text says responses varied and that the lower-response bread differed from person to person, so sourdough did not produce the lower response in most people.

C.why_wrong: The breads matched only on average; individuals responded differently to them, so bread type did affect individual blood sugar.

D.why_wrong: The bacteria were measured before the trial to predict responses; the text does not report any change in them caused by the bread.

sources.what: Korem et al., Cell Metabolism 2017: randomized crossover, one week each of industrial white bread and whole-grain sourdough; no significant differential effects of bread type on clinical parameters; glycemic responses varied between people; the bread inducing the lower response could be predicted from microbiome data before the intervention

items.notes: Area: natural science (nutrition, microbiology). Steps: (1) no average difference but opposite individual responses means the effect is person-specific; (2) prediction from gut bacteria ties it to a personal trait. Participant count dropped (not on the cited page).

fixes: dropped '20' participants (not on the cited page); 'consumed' to 'ate'

band7.why: Two steps (no average difference but opposite individual responses; prediction from gut bacteria) and A, C, D each keep a true piece, but options average about 17 words and only one REV: band 6.

items.subtype: Received view (stylistic change) plus new evidence (air pollution)
items.passage: Over their careers, the British painter Joseph Mallord William Turner and the French painter Claude Monet both moved from crisp, sharply outlined scenes toward hazy, pale compositions in which contours dissolve. This transition has usually been interpreted as an evolution in artistic style.
